title: Disinfection journal: what to record and how to keep service reports
excerpt: The product, concentration, contact time, area treated, and signature: what belongs in the journal. How to store pest-control contractor reports without losing them among accounting files and email.

body.text: A disinfection journal is not just a record that ‘the floor was washed.’ It tracks which product was used, at what concentration, for how long, and where. Inspectors use it to assess whether the facility controls microbes and whether actual use matches the contractor’s report.

items: Area or item: room, workshop, equipment, refrigerator, or vehicle.
Product: trade name, active ingredient, and concentration.
The responsible person and their signature.

body.text: This is a separate document from an external provider covering pest control and disinfection. Do not copy it into the journal; attach it instead. Reports often go missing because they are left with accounting, filed with contracts, or buried in a shared inbox. In an electronic journal, the report is attached directly to the record and stays with it.

body.title: Watch the re-entry interval
body.text: After using many products, production must not resume for 2–4 hours. Violating this requirement can be direct grounds for suspending operations.

Some entries can be automated: scheduled daily treatment of work surfaces can use a standard template that only needs a signature. Unscheduled work and contractor reports should be a separate category, so an inspector can see that routine and responsive treatment are distinguished.
